name: Palace Hotel, San Francisco
positioning: Historic landmark hotel on Market Street in downtown San Francisco, officially Palace Hotel, a Luxury Collection Hotel, San Francisco, pairing original architecture with modern decor
best_for: Travelers who love history, architecture and art
Guests who want a central downtown base steps from Union Square, cable cars and Chinatown

facts.text: The hotel pairs original architecture and authentic elements with classically inspired, modern decor.
The original Palace Hotel was destroyed in the fire that engulfed San Francisco in 1906.
The Pied Piper painting by Maxfield Parrish measures 6 feet by 16 feet and features 27 expressive faces, including Parrish himself as the Pied Piper.
The Green Goddess Crab Salad was created at the Palace Hotel in 1923.
Room carpet and decor pay tribute to California Impressionism.
Rooms have 11-foot ceilings with crown molding.
Every room and suite offers full or partial views of downtown.
Rooms on some floors have TOTO washlets.
The fitness center overlooks the atrium.
The hotel is steps from Union Square, cable cars and Chinatown.
The Concierge team gives curated recommendations, from jazz performances to exhibitions at SFMOMA.

highlights.text: The Garden Court has Italian marble pillars and Austrian crystal chandeliers under a 110-year-old glass dome.
The heated indoor pool has a glass ceiling.
Rooms have a solid oak door with a monogrammed brass doorknob, a signature feature since 1909.
Landmark 18 is a curated museum on the lobby level with details, stories and artifacts from the hotel's history.
The Presidential Suite wraps around a corner of the hotel and overlooks Market Street through arched windows.

considerations.text: The hotel is on Market Street at the border of SoMa and the Financial District, where street life is colorful and guests should stay aware of their surroundings.
WhataHotel notes premium luxury pricing reflecting the high-end positioning.
WhataHotel notes the historic building may have smaller room configurations.
